hints: Recall why copper is an exception, think about the stability of a full 3d subshell compared with the expected 3d9 4s2 arrangement.
Remember which subshell loses electrons first when a transition metal forms a positive ion, the 4s electrons are removed before 3d.
walkthrough:
Start from the expected count**
Copper has atomic number 29, so you have 29 electrons to place. If you followed the simple order you would predict $3d^94s^2$. Keep that in mind, then ask why copper does not do this.

Apply the copper exception**
A completely full $3d^{10}$ subshell is extra stable. One $4s$ electron promotes to $3d$ to give $3s^23p^63d^{10}4s^1$ for the atom. That is the first answer.

Form Cu+ by removing 4s first**
When forming positive ions, $4s$ electrons are always lost before $3d$. Remove the single $4s^1$ electron to leave $3s^23p^63d^{10}$ for $\text{Cu}^+$.

hints: Work out the coordination number first, a linear complex with monodentate ligands must have only two ligands attached to the central metal.
Balance the charges, combine the +1 charge on copper(I) with the charges of the chloride ligands to find the overall charge.
walkthrough:
Picture what linear means**
Linear means bond angle $180^\circ$ with two groups opposite each other. Since $\text{Cl}^-$ is monodentate, each $\text{Cl}^-$ forms one coordinate bond, so two $\text{Cl}^-$ give coordination number 2.

Write the correct formula and charge**
$\text{Cu}^+$ plus $2 \times \text{Cl}^-$ gives $(+1) + (-2) = -1$. So the complex is $[\text{CuCl}_2]^-$, drawn as $\text{Cl}-\text{Cu}-\text{Cl}$ in a straight line.
Final answer: $[\text{CuCl}_2]^-$ shown linear as $\text{Cl}-\text{Cu}-\text{Cl}$ with overall $1-$ charge.

hints: Count the ligands, six identical water ligands around Cu2+ points to the regular six coordinate shape.
Recall the two characteristic bond angles in that six coordinate shape, the adjacent and opposite ligand positions.
walkthrough:
Recognise the six coordinate shape**
$[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ has six monodentate water ligands, so coordination number is 6. The regular arrangement that keeps six groups furthest apart is octahedral.

Draw and label correctly**
Put Cu in the centre with four $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ in the plane (one wedge, one dashed for 3D), one above and one below. Label $90^\circ$ between adjacent $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands and $180^\circ$ between opposite ligands.
Final answer: Octahedral diagram with central Cu surrounded by six $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands, with $90^\circ$ (adjacent) and $180^\circ$ (opposite) angles labelled.

hints: Recall what dilute ammonia does first, it provides OH- and precipitates the copper(II) hydroxide.
Write the precipitation equation starting from [Cu(H2O)6]2+ and adding OH-, balancing waters carefully.
Recall the colour change when excess ammonia redissolves the precipitate to give the soluble ammine complex.
Write the second equation showing Cu(OH)2 reacting with excess NH3 to give the tetraammine complex and OH-.
walkthrough:
Understand reaction 1 as precipitation**
Dropwise $\text{NH}_3(aq)$ acts as a base: $\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$. The $\text{OH}^-$ removes water ligands as $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and precipitates neutral $\text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2$, which you see as a blue solid.

Write the balanced precipitation equation**
$$[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check atoms and charge: $2+$ on each side, balanced.

Understand reaction 2 as redissolving**
In excess $\text{NH}_3$, the precipitate acts as a starting material for ligand exchange. $\text{NH}_3$ ligands replace $\text{OH}^-$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give the soluble deep dark blue tetraammine complex.

Write the complex formation equation**
$$\text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2 + 4\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow [\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^-$$ The observation is a deep royal blue solution, characteristic of $[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^{2+}$ often simplified to $[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$.

Final answer: Reaction 1 observation: blue precipitate / blue solid.
Reaction 1 equation: $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$
Reaction 2 observation: deep / dark / royal blue solution.
Reaction 2 equation: $\text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2 + 4\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow [\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^-$

hints: Focus on what happens to the ligands, water ligands are being swapped for EDTA without change in oxidation state.
walkthrough:
Name the reaction type**
$\text{EDTA}^{4-}$ takes the place of the six water ligands around $\text{Cu}^{2+}$. Whenever one ligand replaces another at the same metal centre, with no redox, call it ligand exchange (or substitution).
Final answer: Ligand exchange / displacement / replacement / substitution.

hints: Write Kstab like a Kc expression but only for the complex formation equilibrium, products over reactants with no water included as it is in excess.
walkthrough:
Build the Kstab expression**
For $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + \text{EDTA}^{4-} \rightleftharpoons [\text{CuEDTA}]^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, omit water. Put the complex concentration on top and multiply the two reactant concentrations below: $$K_{\text{stab}} = \dfrac{[[\text{CuEDTA}]^{2-}]}{[[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}][[\text{EDTA}]^{4-}]}$$

hints: Think about what a very large value like 6.3 x 10^19 tells you about the position of equilibrium and the relative stability of the EDTA complex.
walkthrough:
Interpret the huge number**
$K_{\text{stab}} = 6.3 \times 10^{19}$ is enormous, so the equilibrium lies almost completely to the right. That means $[\text{CuEDTA}]^{2-}$ is very stable compared with the hexaaqua ion.
Final answer: Very stable / more stable than $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$, equilibrium lies far to the right.

hints: Start from the general definition of any ligand in terms of lone pairs and coordinate bonding to a metal.
Add what the prefix bi means for the number of bonds each ethanedioate ion forms.
walkthrough:
Define ligand behaviour**
Picture the ligand as a Lewis base. Each donor atom has a lone pair that it donates into an empty orbital on the metal to form a dative covalent (coordinate) bond.

Explain bidentate**
The prefix bi means two. Ethanedioate $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ uses two oxygen donor atoms, so each ion donates two lone pairs and forms two coordinate bonds to the same metal centre.

Final answer: A ligand that donates lone pairs to form dative / coordinate bonds to the central metal atom / ion.
A bidentate ligand donates two lone pairs / forms two coordinate bonds per ligand.

hints: Calculate the overall charge by adding the 4+ on Zr to the total charge from four ethanedioate ions.
Count the total number of coordinate bonds from four bidentate ligands and compare with the six bonds needed for octahedral.
walkthrough:
Deduce the formula**
$\text{Zr}^{4+}$ plus four $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ gives $(+4) + 4(-2) = -4$. So the ion is $[\text{Zr}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_4]^{4-}$.

Explain the shape**
Each ethanedioate is bidentate, so four ligands give $4 \times 2 = 8$ coordinate bonds. Coordination number is 8. Octahedral geometry requires exactly 6 bonds, so this complex cannot be octahedral.

Final answer: $[\text{Zr}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_4]^{4-}$
Not octahedral because coordination number is 8 / not 6, there are 8 dative bonds to Zr.
